title: Lesson 15: Anomaly Detection - Isolation Forest
text: Anomalies in health data can indicate fraud, rare diseases, sensor errors, or outbreaks. Unsupervised anomaly detection flags unusual cases without labels, useful when labeled anomalies are scarce.

title: Lesson 15: Anomaly Detection - Isolation Forest
text: Anomalies in health data can indicate fraud, rare diseases, sensor errors, or outbreaks. Unsupervised anomaly detection flags unusual cases without labels, useful when labeled anomalies are scarce.

title: Lesson 15: Anomaly Detection - Isolation Forest
text:
Research Question
Can we detect anomalous patients/records in a health dataset, and do flagged cases make clinical sense?

title: Lesson 15: Anomaly Detection - Isolation Forest
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Credit Card Fraud (proxy) or a clinical vitals dataset.

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud (proxy for anomaly detection)
Better clinical: https://physionet.org/ (ICU vitals) or UCI Heart Disease.
Size: varies.
Outcome: anomaly flag (often unavailable -> unsupervised).
Notes: extreme imbalance; evaluate with precision@k.

title: Lesson 15: Anomaly Detection - Isolation Forest
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Isolation Forest (scikit-learn) plus Local Outlier Factor; compare flagged cases.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

df = pd.read_csv("vitals.csv")
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df.select_dtypes(include="number"))
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=42)
df["anomaly"] = iso.fit_predict(X)  # -1 = anomaly
print(df["anomaly"].value_counts())
print(df[df["anomaly"] == -1].head())


Suggested AI prompts

“How does Isolation Forest work intuitively?”
“How do I choose the contamination parameter?”
“How do I evaluate an unsupervised anomaly detector without labels?”



Extensions

Compare with LOF and One-Class SVM.
Inspect top anomalies clinically.
Vary contamination and see stability.

title: Lesson 13: Obesity - Ordinal and Multinomial Regression
text: Obesity is classified into ordered categories (normal, overweight, obese I/II/III). When the outcome is ordinal, ordinal regression respects the ordering and is more efficient than treating categories as nominal.

title: Lesson 13: Obesity - Ordinal and Multinomial Regression
text: Obesity is classified into ordered categories (normal, overweight, obese I/II/III). When the outcome is ordinal, ordinal regression respects the ordering and is more efficient than treating categories as nominal.

title: Lesson 13: Obesity - Ordinal and Multinomial Regression
text:
Research Question
What factors predict obesity level, and does ordinal regression outperform multinomial?

title: Lesson 13: Obesity - Ordinal and Multinomial Regression
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Obesity (or Estimation of Obesity Levels) dataset (UCI).

Link: https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/544/estimation+of+obesity+levels+based+on+eating+habits+and+physical+condition
Size: ~2,100 rows.
Outcome: obesity level (ordered).
Predictors: age, gender, height, weight, eating habits, activity.
Notes: derived from synthetic + real data.

title: Lesson 13: Obesity - Ordinal and Multinomial Regression
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Ordinal logistic regression (mord / statsmodels) vs. multinomial logistic regression.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

df = pd.read_csv("obesity.csv")
X = pd.get_dummies(df.drop(columns=["NObeyesdad"]), drop_first=True)
y = df["NObeyesdad"]
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
multi = LogisticRegression(multi_class="multinomial", max_iter=1000)
print("Multinomial CV acc:", cross_val_score(multi, Xs, y, cv=5).mean())


Suggested AI prompts

“What is the proportional odds assumption in ordinal regression?”
“When should I use multinomial instead of ordinal?”
“How do I evaluate an ordinal classifier beyond accuracy?”



Extensions

Fit an ordinal model (mord.LogisticIT) and compare.
Collapse rare top categories and re-evaluate.
Examine coefficient stability across thresholds.

title: Lesson 11: Causal Inference - Propensity Scores (NHANES)
text: Observational health studies are plagued by confounding. Causal inference methods (propensity scores, matching, weighting) aim to estimate treatment effects as if from a randomized trial. NHANES provides rich, nationally representative health data.

title: Lesson 11: Causal Inference - Propensity Scores (NHANES)
text: Observational health studies are plagued by confounding. Causal inference methods (propensity scores, matching, weighting) aim to estimate treatment effects as if from a randomized trial. NHANES provides rich, nationally representative health data.

title: Lesson 11: Causal Inference - Propensity Scores (NHANES)
text:
Research Question
Does smoking causally affect a biomarker (e.g., CRP / blood pressure), after adjusting for confounders?

title: Lesson 11: Causal Inference - Propensity Scores (NHANES)
text:
Open-Source Dataset
NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey).

Link: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/
Size: thousands per cycle; combine cycles.
Variables: smoking status, demographics, BMI, biomarkers.
Notes: survey weights; handle complex design for population inference.

title: Lesson 11: Causal Inference - Propensity Scores (NHANES)
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Propensity score matching / IPW using logistic regression for the propensity model.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
import numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv("nhanes.csv")  # columns: smoke (0/1), age, sex, bmi, sbp, ...
conf = ["age", "sex", "bmi"]
ps_model = LogisticRegression().fit(df[conf], df["smoke"])
df["ps"] = ps_model.predict_proba(df[conf])[:, 1]
# Nearest-neighbor matching on logit(ps)
logit = np.log(df["ps"]/(1-df["ps"]))
# ... match treated to control
print(df.groupby("smoke")["sbp"].mean())


Suggested AI prompts

“What is a propensity score and what does it balance?”
“How do I check covariate balance after matching?”
“What assumptions (positivity, no unmeasured confounding) are required?”



Extensions

Use inverse probability weighting (IPW) and compare.
Estimate the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT).
Add survey weights for population representativeness.

title: Lesson 9: Cancer Survival - Cox Proportional Hazards
text: Survival analysis models time-to-event outcomes (death, relapse) while handling censoring (patients lost to follow-up). The Cox proportional hazards model is the standard, relating covariates to hazard without assuming a baseline distribution.

title: Lesson 9: Cancer Survival - Cox Proportional Hazards
text: Survival analysis models time-to-event outcomes (death, relapse) while handling censoring (patients lost to follow-up). The Cox proportional hazards model is the standard, relating covariates to hazard without assuming a baseline distribution.

title: Lesson 9: Cancer Survival - Cox Proportional Hazards
text:
Research Question
Which factors affect survival time in cancer patients, and how do we handle censored observations?

title: Lesson 9: Cancer Survival - Cox Proportional Hazards
text:
Open-Source Dataset
METABRIC (breast cancer) or SEER sample.

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/raghadalharbi/breast-cancer-gene-expression-profiles-metabric
Size: ~2,000 patients.
Outcome: overall survival time + event indicator.
Predictors: age, tumor size, grade, ER/PR/HER2 status, treatment.
Notes: censoring ~40%; check proportional hazards assumption.

title: Lesson 9: Cancer Survival - Cox Proportional Hazards
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Cox PH (lifelines CoxPHFitter); evaluate with concordance index.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from lifelines import CoxPHFitter

df = pd.read_csv("metabric.csv")
cols = ["age_at_diagnosis", "tumor_size", "neoplasm_histologic_grade",
        "overall_survival_months", "overall_survival"]
df = df[cols].dropna()
cph = CoxPHFitter()
cph.fit(df, duration_col="overall_survival_months", event_col="overall_survival")
print(cph.summary)
print("C-index:", cph.concordance_index_)


Suggested AI prompts

“What is censoring and why does standard regression fail?”
“Explain the proportional hazards assumption and how to test it.”
“How do I interpret a hazard ratio clinically?”



Extensions

Plot Kaplan-Meier curves by risk group.
Try a random survival forest.
Check for time-varying effects.

title: Lesson 7: Genomics - PCA and Clustering
text: Genomics produces thousands of features (genes) per sample. Unsupervised methods reduce dimensionality and reveal structure: cancer subtypes, cell types, population stratification. PCA and clustering are the workhorses.

title: Lesson 7: Genomics - PCA and Clustering
text: Genomics produces thousands of features (genes) per sample. Unsupervised methods reduce dimensionality and reveal structure: cancer subtypes, cell types, population stratification. PCA and clustering are the workhorses.

title: Lesson 7: Genomics - PCA and Clustering
text:
Research Question
Can gene-expression profiles separate cancer subtypes without labels, and do clusters align with known biology?

title: Lesson 7: Genomics - PCA and Clustering
text:
Open-Source Dataset
TCGA gene expression (via Kaggle or UCSC Xena).

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/crawford/gene-expression (or https://xenabrowser.net/)
Size: hundreds of samples, thousands of genes.
Outcome: cancer type / subtype (for validation only).
Notes: high-dimensional; standardize; consider variance filtering.

title: Lesson 7: Genomics - PCA and Clustering
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
PCA for dimensionality reduction + KMeans / hierarchical clustering; evaluate with silhouette and adjusted Rand index.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

df = pd.read_csv("gene_expression.csv")
X = df.drop(columns=["label"])
y = df["label"]
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
Z = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(Xs)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, random_state=42, n_init=10).fit(Z)
print("ARI:", adjusted_rand_score(y, km.labels_))


Suggested AI prompts

“Why standardize before PCA on gene expression?”
“How many principal components should I keep, and how do I decide?”
“When should I use hierarchical clustering instead of KMeans?”



Extensions

Plot PC1 vs PC2 colored by true label.
Try UMAP and compare with PCA.
Filter to top-variance genes and re-cluster.

title: Lesson 5: Mental Health Text - Naive Bayes and NLP
text: Mental health conditions are often first expressed in language. Analyzing text from forums, surveys, or clinical notes can support screening and triage, but raises serious privacy and ethics concerns. Naive Bayes remains a strong, interpretable baseline for text classification.

title: Lesson 5: Mental Health Text - Naive Bayes and NLP
text: Mental health conditions are often first expressed in language. Analyzing text from forums, surveys, or clinical notes can support screening and triage, but raises serious privacy and ethics concerns. Naive Bayes remains a strong, interpretable baseline for text classification.

title: Lesson 5: Mental Health Text - Naive Bayes and NLP
text:
Research Question
Can short text posts be classified into mental-health categories, and how far does a simple Naive Bayes model go?

title: Lesson 5: Mental Health Text - Naive Bayes and NLP
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Reddit Mental Health (or CLPsych shared tasks).

Link: https://zenodo.org/records/3941387 (Reddit mental health dataset) or CLPsych datasets.
Size: varies; tens of thousands of posts.
Outcome: condition label (e.g., depression, anxiety, none).
Notes: anonymized; handle with care; not for clinical use.

title: Lesson 5: Mental Health Text - Naive Bayes and NLP
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Multinomial Naive Bayes with TF-IDF features (scikit-learn).


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

df = pd.read_csv("mental_health_posts.csv")  # columns: text, label
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(df["text"], df["label"],
                                       test_size=0.2, stratify=df["label"], random_state=42)
pipe = Pipeline([("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", max_features=5000)),
                 ("nb", MultinomialNB())])
pipe.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(classification_report(yte, pipe.predict(Xte)))


Suggested AI prompts

“Why is Naive Bayes ‘naive’, and why does it still work for text?”
“How do I inspect which words drive each class prediction?”
“What are the ethical risks of classifying mental health from social media?”



Extensions

Try logistic regression with TF-IDF and compare.
Add bigrams and tune min_df.
Examine errors: which posts are hardest?

title: Lesson 3: Breast Cancer Classification - Support Vector Machines
text: Breast cancer is among the most common cancers in women. Early detection via imaging and pathology dramatically improves outcomes. The Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset contains features computed from digitized images of fine-needle aspirates, making it a clean testbed for classification algorithms.

title: Lesson 3: Breast Cancer Classification - Support Vector Machines
text: Breast cancer is among the most common cancers in women. Early detection via imaging and pathology dramatically improves outcomes. The Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset contains features computed from digitized images of fine-needle aspirates, making it a clean testbed for classification algorithms.

title: Lesson 3: Breast Cancer Classification - Support Vector Machines
text:
Research Question
Can cell-nucleus measurements distinguish malignant from benign tumors, and how does an SVM compare to simpler models?

title: Lesson 3: Breast Cancer Classification - Support Vector Machines
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Wisconsin Breast Cancer (Diagnostic) (UCI / scikit-learn built-in).

Link: https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast+cancer+wisconsin+diagnostic
Also: sklearn.datasets.load_breast_cancer().
Size: 569 rows, 30 features.
Outcome: diagnosis (M/B).
Notes: features are means, standard errors, and “worst” values of 10 nucleus characteristics.

title: Lesson 3: Breast Cancer Classification - Support Vector Machines
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Support Vector Machine with RBF kernel, plus linear SVM and logistic regression for comparison; scaling is critical.


Starter code
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, roc_auc_score

data = load_breast_cancer()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(data.data, data.target, test_size=0.25,
                                       stratify=data.target, random_state=42)
pipe = Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("svm", SVC(kernel="rbf", probability=True))])
pipe.fit(Xtr, ytr)
proba = pipe.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
print("AUC:", roc_auc_score(yte, proba))
print(classification_report(yte, pipe.predict(Xte)))


Suggested AI prompts

“Why must features be standardized before an SVM? What happens if I skip it?”
“What do the support vectors represent intuitively?”
“How do I tune C and gamma, and what does each control?”



Extensions

Grid-search C and gamma; plot the validation curve.
Compare RBF vs. linear kernel; when is linear enough?
Inspect misclassified cases and their feature values.

title: Lesson 1: Cardiovascular Disease Risk - Logistic Regression
text: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. Risk factors such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, and diabetes are well established, and clinicians routinely combine them into risk scores (e.g., the Framingham Risk Score). Machine learning can reproduce and extend these scores, but interpretability matters: a model that a physician cannot explain will not be adopted.

title: Lesson 1: Cardiovascular Disease Risk - Logistic Regression
text: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. Risk factors such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, and diabetes are well established, and clinicians routinely combine them into risk scores (e.g., the Framingham Risk Score). Machine learning can reproduce and extend these scores, but interpretability matters: a model that a physician cannot explain will not be adopted.

title: Lesson 1: Cardiovascular Disease Risk - Logistic Regression
text:
Research Question
Can routine clinical measurements predict a patient’s 10-year risk of coronary heart disease (CHD), and which factors dominate that risk?

title: Lesson 1: Cardiovascular Disease Risk - Logistic Regression
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Framingham Heart Study dataset (Kaggle mirror of the classic teaching dataset).

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/aasheesh200/framingham-heart-study-dataset
Size: ~4,240 rows, 15 columns.
Outcome: TenYearCHD (binary).
Predictors: age, sex, education, smoking status, cigs/day, BP meds, prevalent stroke, hypertension, diabetes, total cholesterol, BMI, heart rate, glucose.
Notes: missing values (~6%); class imbalance (~15% positive). A good dataset for practicing imputation and threshold selection.

title: Lesson 1: Cardiovascular Disease Risk - Logistic Regression
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Logistic regression (scikit-learn LogisticRegression, statsmodels Logit). Start simple, then add interactions.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, classification_report
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

df = pd.read_csv("framingham.csv")
X = df.drop(columns=["TenYearCHD"])
y = df["TenYearCHD"]
X = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(X)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced")
model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
proba = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
print("AUC:", roc_auc_score(yte, proba))
print(classification_report(yte, (proba > 0.5).astype(int)))


Suggested AI prompts

“Explain the odds ratio for each coefficient in this logistic regression in plain clinical language.”
“How should I choose a decision threshold when false negatives (missed CHD) are costlier than false positives?”
“Compare class_weight=‘balanced’ vs. adjusting the threshold; which is more defensible clinically?”



Extensions

Add an interaction term (age x smoking) and test significance.
Plot a calibration curve; does the model over/under-predict?
Compare with a random forest; where do they disagree?

How to frame a health research question in a way a model can answer.

Each lesson has four parts:

Introduction to the Domain — background and why the problem matters.
Research Question — a precise, testable question.
Open-Source Dataset — a public data source with discussion and a link.

title: About this course
section: A note on responsible ML in health
text:
A note on responsible ML in health
These exercises are educational. Health models can harm real people if misused. Always:

Validate on held-out and, ideally, external data.
Examine performance across subgroups (fairness).
Involve clinicians and domain experts.
Never deploy a model for patient care without proper regulatory and ethical review.

Responsible use
Health data carries real-world consequences. Models built in these exercises are educational and must not be used for clinical decision-making. Always validate on independent data, examine fairness across subgroups, and involve domain experts.

title: Lesson 2: Diabetes Prediction - Random Forest
text: Type 2 diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease whose incidence is rising globally. Early identification of at-risk individuals enables lifestyle intervention. The classic Pima Indians Diabetes dataset is small but ideal for learning tree-based methods and feature importance.

title: Lesson 2: Diabetes Prediction - Random Forest
text: Type 2 diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease whose incidence is rising globally. Early identification of at-risk individuals enables lifestyle intervention. The classic Pima Indians Diabetes dataset is small but ideal for learning tree-based methods and feature importance.

title: Lesson 2: Diabetes Prediction - Random Forest
text:
Research Question
Which clinical measurements best predict diabetes onset, and can a random forest outperform a single decision tree while remaining interpretable?

title: Lesson 2: Diabetes Prediction - Random Forest
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Pima Indians Diabetes Database (UCI / Kaggle).

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/uciml/pima-indians-diabetes-database
Size: 768 rows, 8 features + outcome.
Features: pregnancies, glucose, blood pressure, skin thickness, insulin, BMI, diabetes pedigree function, age.
Outcome: Outcome (0/1).
Notes: zeros encode missing values in several columns; handle before modeling.

title: Lesson 2: Diabetes Prediction - Random Forest
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Random Forest classifier (scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier), plus a single decision tree for comparison and SHAP for interpretation.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

df = pd.read_csv("diabetes.csv")
cols = ["Glucose", "BloodPressure", "SkinThickness", "Insulin", "BMI"]
df[cols] = df[cols].replace(0, pd.NA)
X = df.drop(columns=["Outcome"]); y = df["Outcome"]
X = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(X)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42)
dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=42)
print("RF CV AUC:", cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean())
print("DT CV AUC:", cross_val_score(dt, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean())


Suggested AI prompts

“Explain the difference between Gini importance and permutation importance; which should I trust here?”
“How do I read a SHAP summary plot for this random forest?”
“Why might glucose dominate, and what does that imply for screening?”



Extensions

Tune max_depth and min_samples_leaf with a grid search.
Add SHAP values and check for interactions (glucose x BMI).
Try class balancing and report sensitivity at 90% specificity.

title: Lesson 4: Hospital Readmission - Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
text: Unplanned hospital readmissions are costly and often preventable. Predicting which patients will return within 30 days lets hospitals target discharge planning and follow-up. The data is messy: mixed types, missingness, and rare outcomes.

title: Lesson 4: Hospital Readmission - Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
text: Unplanned hospital readmissions are costly and often preventable. Predicting which patients will return within 30 days lets hospitals target discharge planning and follow-up. The data is messy: mixed types, missingness, and rare outcomes.

title: Lesson 4: Hospital Readmission - Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
text:
Research Question
Can we predict 30-day readmission from administrative and clinical data, and does gradient boosting beat logistic regression?

title: Lesson 4: Hospital Readmission - Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Diabetes 130-US Hospitals (1999-2008) (UCI).

Link: https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/296/diabetes+130-us+hospitals+for+years+1999-2008
Size: ~100k encounters.
Outcome: readmitted (<30 days vs. not).
Predictors: demographics, diagnoses (ICD-9), medications, lab results, length of stay.
Notes: de-identified; multi-level (patient/encounter).

title: Lesson 4: Hospital Readmission - Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
XGBoost (xgboost.XGBClassifier) with careful handling of categoricals and imbalance.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

df = pd.read_csv("diabetic_data.csv")
y = (df["readmitted"] == "<30").astype(int)
X = df.drop(columns=["readmitted", "encounter_id", "patient_nbr"])
cat = X.select_dtypes(include="object").columns
X[cat] = OrdinalEncoder(handle_unknown="use_encoded_value", unknown_value=-1).fit_transform(X[cat])
X = X.fillna(-1)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)

model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=400, max_depth=5, learning_rate=0.05,
                      scale_pos_weight=(ytr==0).sum()/(ytr==1).sum(), eval_metric="auc")
model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("AUC:", roc_auc_score(yte, model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]))


Suggested AI prompts

“How do I handle high-cardinality diagnosis codes in XGBoost?”
“Explain scale_pos_weight vs. threshold tuning for imbalanced readmission.”
“What leakage risks exist in hospital readmission data?”



Extensions

Add SHAP and identify top drivers of readmission.
Group K-fold by patient to avoid leakage.
Compare with a simple logistic regression baseline.

title: Lesson 6: COVID-19 - Time-Series Forecasting
text: Pandemics unfold over time, and forecasting cases, hospitalizations, and deaths informs policy. Time-series methods capture trend, seasonality, and shocks, but COVID-19 broke many assumptions (structural breaks, reporting delays).

title: Lesson 6: COVID-19 - Time-Series Forecasting

Research Question
Can we forecast COVID-19 cases for a region, and how do classical (ARIMA) and modern (Prophet) methods compare?

title: Lesson 6: COVID-19 - Time-Series Forecasting
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Our World in Data COVID-19 dataset.

Link: https://github.com/owid/covid-19-data
Daily CSV: https://covid.ourworldindata.org/data/owid-covid-data.csv
Size: country-day rows since 2020.
Variables: new cases, deaths, tests, vaccinations, hospitalizations.
Notes: reporting delays and definition changes; smooth/aggregate.

title: Lesson 6: COVID-19 - Time-Series Forecasting
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
ARIMA (statsmodels) and Prophet; also try simple baselines.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

df = pd.read_csv("owid-covid-data.csv")
sub = df[df["location"] == "United States"][["date", "new_cases_smoothed"]].dropna()
sub["date"] = pd.to_datetime(sub["date"])
sub = sub.set_index("date").asfreq("D")
y = sub["new_cases_smoothed"]
train, test = y.iloc[:-30], y.iloc[-30:]
model = ARIMA(train, order=(2, 1, 2)).fit()
fc = model.forecast(steps=30)
print(fc.head())


Suggested AI prompts

“How do I choose ARIMA (p,d,q) orders? Explain ACF/PACF.”
“What is Prophet’s changepoint prior scale and how does it affect forecasts?”
“Why might a naive baseline beat a complex model during a pandemic?”



Extensions

Add Prophet with holidays and compare MAPE.
Forecast hospitalizations instead of cases.
Compute prediction intervals and check coverage.

title: Lesson 8: Medical Imaging - Convolutional Neural Networks
text: Medical imaging (X-rays, CT, MRI) is a leading application of deep learning. CNNs can detect pneumonia, fractures, and tumors, but require large datasets, careful validation, and attention to bias and shortcut learning.

title: Lesson 8: Medical Imaging - Convolutional Neural Networks

Research Question
Can a CNN classify chest X-rays as normal vs. pneumonia, and what are the pitfalls?

title: Lesson 8: Medical Imaging - Convolutional Neural Networks

Open-Source Dataset
NIH ChestX-ray14 / Kaggle Chest X-Ray Images (Pneumonia).

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/paultimothymooney/chest-xray-pneumonia
Size: ~5,800 images.
Outcome: NORMAL / PNEUMONIA.

title: Lesson 8: Medical Imaging - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Transfer learning with a pretrained ResNet (torchvision), fine-tuned on chest X-rays.


Starter code
import torch
from torchvision import models, transforms
from torchvision.datasets import ImageFolder
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

tfm = transforms.Compose([transforms.Resize((224, 224)),
                          transforms.ToTensor(),
                          transforms.Normalize([0.485, 0.456, 0.406], [0.229, 0.224, 0.225])])
train = ImageFolder("chest_xray/train", transform=tfm)
loader = DataLoader(train, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)
model = models.resnet18(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1")
model.fc = torch.nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, 2)
print("ready")


Suggested AI prompts

“Explain transfer learning: why start from ImageNet for medical images?”
“How do I avoid data leakage from patient-level duplicates?”
“What is ‘shortcut learning’ in medical imaging and how do I detect it?”



Extensions

Add Grad-CAM to visualize attention.
Evaluate by subgroup (age, sex) if available.
Compare with a simple baseline (image mean intensity).

title: Lesson 10: Drug Discovery - Random Forest on Molecules
text: Drug discovery screens thousands of compounds for activity. Molecular descriptors (physicochemical properties) can predict toxicity or activity, accelerating prioritization. Tree-based models handle mixed, high-dimensional descriptors well.

title: Lesson 10: Drug Discovery - Random Forest on Molecules
text: Drug discovery screens thousands of compounds for activity. Molecular descriptors (physicochemical properties) can predict toxicity or activity, accelerating prioritization. Tree-based models handle mixed, high-dimensional descriptors well.

title: Lesson 10: Drug Discovery - Random Forest on Molecules
text:
Research Question
Can molecular descriptors predict compound toxicity (Tox21), and which properties matter most?

title: Lesson 10: Drug Discovery - Random Forest on Molecules
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Tox21 / MoleculeNet.

Link: https://moleculenet.org/datasets-1 (Tox21)
Also: https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem
Size: ~8k compounds, 12 toxicity endpoints.
Outcome: binary toxicity per endpoint.
Notes: SMILES strings; need featurization (RDKit).

title: Lesson 10: Drug Discovery - Random Forest on Molecules
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
Random Forest on RDKit descriptors (or Morgan fingerprints).


Starter code
import pandas as pd
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import Descriptors
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

df = pd.read_csv("tox21.csv")
def feats(smi):
    m = Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi)
    return [Descriptors.MolWt(m), Descriptors.MolLogP(m), Descriptors.TPSA(m)]
X = df["smiles"].apply(feats).tolist()
y = df["NR-AR"]
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42)
print("CV AUC:", cross_val_score(rf, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean())


Suggested AI prompts

“What are Morgan fingerprints vs. physicochemical descriptors?”
“How do I avoid data leakage across similar molecules (scaffold split)?”
“Why is AUC-PR more informative than AUC-ROC for rare toxicity?”



Extensions

Use scaffold splitting for honest evaluation.
Try gradient boosting and compare.
Visualize important descriptors.

title: Lesson 12: Healthcare Costs - Generalized Linear Models
text: Healthcare spending is right-skewed and heteroscedastic: a few patients dominate costs. Generalized linear models (GLMs) with appropriate families (Gamma, Tweedie) and link functions model such outcomes better than ordinary least squares.

title: Lesson 12: Healthcare Costs - Generalized Linear Models
text: Healthcare spending is right-skewed and heteroscedastic: a few patients dominate costs. Generalized linear models (GLMs) with appropriate families (Gamma, Tweedie) and link functions model such outcomes better than ordinary least squares.

title: Lesson 12: Healthcare Costs - Generalized Linear Models
text:
Research Question
What drives individual medical charges, and which GLM family fits cost data best?

title: Lesson 12: Healthcare Costs - Generalized Linear Models
text:
Open-Source Dataset
Medical Cost Personal dataset.

Link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mirichoi0218/insurance
Size: 1,338 rows.
Outcome: charges.
Predictors: age, sex, BMI, children, smoker, region.
Notes: strong smoker effect; right skew.

title: Lesson 12: Healthcare Costs - Generalized Linear Models
text:
Practical Exercise

Model to explore
GLM with Gamma family and log link (statsmodels), plus OLS and Tweedie for comparison.


Starter code
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

df = pd.read_csv("insurance.csv")
df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["sex", "smoker", "region"], drop_first=True)
X = sm.add_constant(df.drop(columns=["charges"]))
y = df["charges"]
glm = sm.GLM(y, X, family=sm.families.Gamma(link=sm.families.links.Log())).fit()
print(glm.summary())
print("AIC:", glm.aic)


Suggested AI prompts

“Why is OLS inappropriate for cost data? Explain skewness and heteroscedasticity.”
“What does the Gamma family assume, and when is Tweedie better?”
“How do I interpret coefficients with a log link (multiplicative effects)?”



Extensions

Compare AIC across families.
Add an interaction (smoker x BMI).
Predict and plot residuals vs. fitted.
